title: Remoting: run it on the servers
summary: Invoke-Command over SSH and WinRM, fan-out to many hosts, sessions, $using:, and why remote results are deserialized snapshots without methods.

steps.title: Invoke-Command: one command, many machines
body: PowerShell remoting runs a script block **on** other machines and brings the **results** back as objects:
```powershell
# Windows, in a domain: WinRM (ports 5985/5986), Kerberos, -ComputerName
Invoke-Command -ComputerName web01, web02 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service W3SVC }
# Anywhere (Linux, macOS, Windows with OpenSSH Server): SSH, keys, -HostName
Invoke-Command -HostName web01, web02 -UserName deploy -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File }
| | WinRM (`-ComputerName`) | SSH (`-HostName`) |
| Set up on the target | `Enable-PSRemoting` (admin), usually by Group Policy | sshd with `Subsystem powershell /usr/bin/pwsh -sshs` |
| Authentication | Kerberos in a domain, `-Credential` | SSH keys (`-KeyFilePath`) or a password |
| Works with | Windows PowerShell 5.1 and 7 on Windows | PowerShell 7 on every OS |
- It runs on all hosts **at once** (`-ThrottleLimit`, default 32), and every result carries a **`PSComputerName`**
property, so `Group-Object PSComputerName` or `Sort-Object PSComputerName` just works.
- **`Enter-PSSession web01`** gives an interactive remote prompt; `New-PSSession` keeps a connection open for
several `Invoke-Command -Session $s` calls (much faster than reconnecting each time).
- Local variables are not visible remotely: pass them with **`$using:days`** (or `-ArgumentList`).
This machine runs sshd with the PowerShell subsystem; the names `web01` and `web02` both point at it, so the
remoting is real, and both "servers" show the same files.

steps.prompt: `$days = 30; Invoke-Command -HostName web01 { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-$days) }` returns **every** file, even today's. Why?
options: `$days` does not exist on web01, so it is `$null`, `AddDays(-$null)` is now, and every file is older than now: use `$using:days`
Where-Object does not work in remote sessions
steps.explain: The script block runs in a new session on the remote machine with none of your variables. With `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` inside the block it would have failed loudly instead. Imagine that line feeding `Remove-Item`.

steps.title: Log usage across the web servers
prompt: Using **remoting over SSH** (`Invoke-Command -HostName ... -UserName learner`, your key is already set up), collect
from **web01** and **web02** how many files `/srv/logs/app` holds and their total size, in one `Invoke-Command`.
Export `~/answers/log-usage.csv` with the columns **`Server`**, **`Files`**, **`Bytes`**, one row per server, sorted

checks.name: one row per server with files and bytes
cmd: if not os.path.exists(p): sys.exit('~/answers/log-usage.csv does not exist yet')
if cols != ['Server', 'Files', 'Bytes']: sys.exit(f'columns are {cols}, expected Server, Files, Bytes')
files = [os.path.join('/srv/logs/app', f) for f in os.listdir('/srv/logs/app')]
want = [(s, str(len(files)), str(sum(os.path.getsize(f) for f in files))) for s in ('web01', 'web02')]
got = [(r['Server'], r['Files'], r['Bytes'].split('.')[0]) for r in rows]
checks.fail: Not quite (see what the check found).

checks.name: the data came over SSH remoting

hints: Try one first: `Invoke-Command -HostName web01 -UserName learner -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File }`.
Measure on the server, bring back only the numbers: `-ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Measure-Object Length -Sum }` returns `Count` and `Sum`, plus `PSComputerName`.

`... | Sort-Object PSComputerName | Select-Object @{ n = 'Server'; e = { $_.PSComputerName } }, @{ n = 'Files'; e = { $_.Count } }, @{ n = 'Bytes'; e = { $_.Sum } } | Export-Csv ~/answers/log-usage.csv`
solution: $usage = Invoke-Command -HostName web01, web02 -UserName learner -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum }

$usage | Sort-Object PSComputerName | Select-Object @{ n = 'Server'; e = { $_.PSComputerName } }, @{ n = 'Files'; e = { $_.Count } }, @{ n = 'Bytes'; e = { $_.Sum } } | Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/log-usage.csv
explain: Do the filtering and measuring **remotely** and bring back small results: a `Measure-Object` row crosses the
network in bytes, while a list of 100,000 `FileInfo` objects is serialised one by one. Same idea as "filter left"

steps.title: Remote results are snapshots
body: Objects that come back from another machine are **serialised** to XML and rebuilt locally as
`Deserialized.System.IO.FileInfo` and friends: they have the **properties** (values at the time) but **no methods**
and no live connection to the remote object.
```powershell
$files = Invoke-Command -HostName web01 { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File }
$files[0].Delete()
# Method invocation failed because [Deserialized.System.IO.FileInfo] does not contain a method named 'Delete'.
So **act remotely**: put the `Remove-Item`, `Restart-Service` or `Stop-Process` *inside* the script block. And
`-WhatIf` goes in there too, so a dry run on 50 servers is one line:
```powershell
Invoke-Command -HostName $servers -UserName deploy -ScriptBlock {
Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-$using:days) |
Remove-Item -WhatIf:$using:dryRun
One Windows-only trap to know by name: the **Kerberos double hop**. From a WinRM session on server A you cannot
reach a file share on server B with your credentials (A is not allowed to pass them on). Use resource-based
constrained delegation, or connect to B directly.

steps.title: Clean old logs on both servers, remotely
prompt: On **web01 and web02**, delete the files in `/srv/logs/app` last changed more than **`$days` = 30** days ago, with
one `Invoke-Command` over SSH. Set `$days = 30` in your session and pass it with `$using:`. Do a `-WhatIf` run first
and read what it would delete. (Both names are this machine, so the second server finds the files already gone.)

checks.name: only the recent logs are left
checks.fail: `/srv/logs/app` should keep `api-1.log`, `api-2.log` and `worker.log` (3, 12 and 1 days old) and lose the three older than 30 days.

hints: `$days = 30`, then `Invoke-Command -HostName web01, web02 -UserName learner -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-$using:days) }` lists them.
Add `| Remove-Item -WhatIf` inside the script block for the dry run.
solution: Invoke-Command -HostName web01, web02 -UserName learner -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-$using:days) | Remove-Item -WhatIf }
Invoke-Command -HostName web01, web02 -UserName learner -ScriptBlock { Get-ChildItem /srv/logs/app -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-$using:days) | Remove-Item }
steps.explain: The `-WhatIf` output comes back from each server, so you review the plan for the whole fleet in one place. On Windows, Just Enough Administration (JEA) endpoints go a step further: a remoting endpoint that only allows a few named commands, run as a privileged virtual account, so operators can clean logs without being admins.
